Subject: Metering behavior in pilot — how are long generations counted?

Hi Kimberly,

Quick question as we prepare our integration test for the pilot: we have a usage pattern where users send very short prompts (8–40 tokens) and the model returns long synthesized outputs (often 800–2,400 tokens).

Two things we'd like clarity on before go-live:
- Do you bill every generated token at the same granularity as the prompt tokens (i.e., per-token with no minimum), or is there a minimum per-call/stream that would inflate the effective cost for many short prompts?
- If multiple short user messages are received within a short time, does Redwood amortize context across those requests (we're thinking of a customer chat window where assistant messages are long but user messages are short).

We ran a quick sample and the invoice looked slightly higher than our rough count — wondering where the delta comes from (rounding / minimums / prefix amortization?).

I attached a CSV sample of a few sessions (acme_metering_sample.csv) — would love a simple worked example we can point to in our SRE tests.

Thanks,
Jared

Hi Jared — thanks for the sample, this is a great callout.

Short answer: we bill for actual tokens consumed (prompt + generated) but there are two practical meter behaviors that can create the delta you saw. I'll summarize and then loop in internal ops for exact sample calculations.

What can create the delta:
- Rounding quantum: by default we round per-request to the nearest 1 token (no fractional tokens) — so negligible.
- Per-call microfloor: streaming mode historically had a small per-chunk floor to avoid extremely high cardinality (we typically set this very low, e.g., 3–5 tokens).
- Session amortization: when requests reuse the same KV cache/prefix within an amortization window we avoid recharging the full context every time — but only certain prefixes qualify (session pinned context).

Proposed next steps:
- I'll ask ops to run your CSV against the pilot metering logic and return a worked example.
- If the microfloor is driving >1.5% of billed units for you, we can discuss a temporary concession for the pilot period.

Attached is a quick summary I used internally (will follow with more detail).

Best,

Subject: Re: Metering behavior in pilot — example calculations

Hi all — ran the CSV locally against the pilot metering logic and here's a compact worked example and the rules I used.

Assumptions/Rules used:
- Billable token = prompt_tokens + generated_tokens (no hidden multipliers).
- Token granularity: 1 token (we don't bill fractions).
- Streaming microfloor: minimum 3 tokens billed per streaming chunk. If a generation is streamed across N chunks we apply floor per chunk; typical chunk size ~64 tokens for our streaming pipeline.
- Session amortization window: 45 minutes. If multiple requests share the same pinned prefix (session id) and happen within 45 minutes, the shared prefix is charged once; ephemeral user prompts are billed fully.

Worked examples (from your sample):
1) Session A: user prompt 18 tokens; assistant generates 1,200 tokens streamed across 19 chunks (~64 tokens per chunk). Billable tokens = 18 + 1200 = 1218. Streaming floors applied per chunk are not material here because each chunk exceeds the 3-token floor.
2) Session B (chat window): sequence of three quick user messages within 2 minutes (10, 12, 9 tokens) that reuse a pinned prefix (shared system prompt 1,100 tokens). With amortization: the 1,100-token prefix is charged once, plus the three prompt+generation costs. If we had billed per-call without amortization you'd see the 1,100 repeated.
3) Tiny prompt case: user prompt 4 tokens, assistant generates 6 tokens in a single streamed chunk -> without floor you'd bill 10 tokens; with microfloor you'd bill max(3,6) for the chunk, so still 10. But if assistant generated 1 token in a single chunk you'd hit the 3-token microfloor leading to a 2-token rounding delta.

Aggregate impact: over your CSV sample the microfloor contributed ~0.9% extra billed tokens; rounding to per-token (no fractions) contributed <0.1%. The big savings come from amortization of pinned prefixes — in your workload that explains most of the variability.

If the customer wants, we can:
- Move microfloor to a per-session basis for the pilot (i.e., apply microfloor once per session rather than per chunk) — but that requires a code-path toggle and a short lead time.
- Offer a 90-day concession cap (as Sergio suggested) to keep their effective cost near nominal during onboarding.

Let me know what to confirm for the pitch to Acme.

— Rishi

Jared — thanks for the patience; pulling the pieces together here so your SREs have a single reference.

What Redwood will commit for the Acme Health pilot:
- Metering baseline: billed tokens = prompt + generated tokens, rounded up to the nearest token.
- Streaming microfloor: default = 3 tokens per chunk; for the pilot we will apply microfloor once per session (not per chunk) to avoid pathological deltas for many tiny turns.
- Amortization: pinned prefixes (session/system prompts) amortize over a 45-minute window.
- Pilot concession: Redwood will cap rounding/microfloor overhead at 2% across the first 90 days of the pilot; if measured overhead >2% we will issue a credit equal to the excess (max credit = 5% of pilot spend).
